steps.name: prompt
steps.text: Write the introduction for my paper on learning approximate Nash equilibria in n-player Markov games, applied to dynamic pricing. It should cover the dynamic pricing / market oligopoly background and related work on multi-agent MDPs, and finish with our contributions.

steps.name: skeleton_outline
steps.text:
- Opening: deep RL for multi-agent competitive MDPs is under-explored; Nash equilibria; dynamic pricing as the application
## 1.1 Market Oligopoly

- Our market setup

steps.name: detailed_outline
steps.text:
- Opening
  - deep RL for single player MDPs: well researched; novel deep RL for multi-agent competitive MDPs: relatively few
  - challenge: competing objectives; Nash equilibria often computationally intractable; agents can't just maximize own Q functions
  - Nash equilibria in Markov Games useful for dynamic pricing (online eCommerce marketplaces)
  - dynamic pricing game: multiple firms compete for market share of their product on the same online platform
  - model: modified Bertrand oligopoly, marginal cost of production 0, probabilistic purchasing behaviour

## 1.1 Market Oligopoly
- Nash pricing and prior dynamic pricing work
  - dynamic pricing: adversarial advantage + higher profit margins for platform firms, esp. online commerce
  - pricing strategy should consider other firms' actions -> Nash equilibrium policies over unilateral reward maximization
  - prior work: deep RL for dynamic pricing, but single agent revenue maximization, no multi-agent Nash
  - prior work: stochastic dynamic programming in simulated environment, estimate demand, maximize expected profit; no market equilibrium
  - prior work: parametric demand functions with unknown parameters; no Nash, no effect of previous pricing on demand
  - desideratum to compute/promote Nash equilibria; applicable to e.g. Amazon auto pricing (automated pricing algorithm)
- Demand learning literature
  - many works: unknown demand function, learn price-demand relationship
  - myopic Bayesian policy -> incomplete learning, poor profit performance
  - joint pricing + inventory problem, price-sensitive demand learned with Bayesian dynamic program
  - non-parametric methods: pricing strategy balancing exploration vs exploitation
  - black-box demand approximated from experience replay + live online testing in RL framework (same deep RL work as above)
  - two sub-problems in oligopolies: (1) optimization - Nash policy given demand parameters, (2) learning the demand parameters
  - parametric approaches using maximum likelihood for unknown demand parameters
  - multiple products: assortment pricing with multinomial logit regression; limited inventory: Multi-Armed Bandits effective
  - gaps: past pricing actions influencing future demand ignored; no competing firms aiming for Nash
- Our market setup
  - demand market where past pricing affects future market demand, in a market competition
  - multi-agent MDP; state transition driven by joint pricing actions of all players (firms)
  - simplifications: unlimited inventory per firm, single product, no substitutes

## 1.2 Multi-agent Markov Decision Processes
- Nash equilibria in Markov Games; oracle setting
  - Markov Games (MG's): important when agents self-interested, exact/approximate Nash desired
  - Nash computation hard: enormous joint state action space; approximations to the search exist
  - multiple Nash equilibria complicate the solution; some more desirable than others
  - approximate search: needs prior knowledge of joint reward function, often limited to two players, best response function
  - our payoff function as an oracle: parametric form known, agents don't know how rewards are generated
  - state visible to agents; state transition function unknown
  - demand parameters + Nash equilibria known for experimentation -> no pre-period model fitting; compare to theoretical solution, not empirical estimate
- Model-based vs model-free solvers
  - model-based approaches: provably find existence of a Nash equilibrium
  - we want model-free: no knowledge of reward or transition function
  - model-free algorithm for competitive MDP's when an external party can alter environment parameters - not always the case in market economics
  - model-free decentralized deep learning framework, agent blind to others' actions, proven Nash convergence
  - convergent solution for zero-sum MG's via entropy-regularization
  - both of the last two impose theoretical restrictions on the MG for convergence
  - provably convergent MG solver for imperfect information, restricted to two agents
  - our goal: approximate solution to a full information MG for N agents
- Contributions
  - methodology for Deep Q Learning, extended to multi-agent reinforcement learning (MARL) with a Nash equilibrium objective
  - based on two earlier Nash-objective methods; the first is theoretically sound but its Nash equilibrium function is often intractable
  - -> approximation methods to compute a Nash equilibrium

steps.name: partial_draft
steps.text:
Deep reinforcement learning has been used a lot to solve single player Markov Decision Processes and this is fairly well researched in machine learning today, but there are relatively few works that apply novel deep reinforcement learning methods to multi-agent competitive MDP's. The challenge is mainly that the objectives compete and we have to solve for Nash equilibria, which are often computationally intractable, in a competitive setting where the agents cannot just maximize their own Q functions. Nash equilibria in Markov Games are especially useful for dynamic pricing, which is a well-known problem in online eCommerce marketplaces today. In a dynamic pricing game there are multiple firms that compete for market share of their product on the same online platform. We model this market with a modified version of Bertrand oligopoly, where the marginal cost of production is 0 and where the purchasing behaviour is probabilistic.

## 1.1 Market Oligopoly

Dynamic pricing gives platform firms an adversarial advantage and increases profit margins in a competitive economy, especially in online commerce industries today. Ideally a firm's pricing strategy should take into account the actions of the other firms, and this is the justification for using Nash equilibrium policies instead of unilateral reward maximization policies. One earlier work modelled the dynamic pricing problem using deep reinforcement learning, but it focused mainly on single agent revenue maximization and did not solve for multi-agent Nash equilibria. Another work applies stochastic dynamic programming in a simulated environment to estimate consumer demand and maximize expected profit, but it does not consider the equilibrium solution of the market. Others model market demand with parametric functions that have unknown parameters, but they do not consider a Nash equilibrium, and they also do not consider the effect of previous pricing actions on demand. So in almost all of the recent research on dynamic pricing under uncertainty there is a desideratum to compute and promote Nash equilibria for market pricing strategies. These kinds of strategies can be applied to eCommerce platforms like Amazon auto pricing, so that firms can opt for an automated pricing algorithm.

A large part of the dynamic pricing literature has assumed that the demand function is unknown and tried to learn the relationship between price and demand. It was shown that a myopic Bayesian policy can lead to incomplete learning and poor profit performance. A joint pricing and inventory problem has also been studied, where the price-sensitive demand is learned using a Bayesian dynamic program. Many recent studies are about non-parametric methods. For example, one pricing strategy balances the trade-off between exploration and exploitation. Also, in the deep reinforcement learning work mentioned above the demand function was a black box system and the demand was approximated from experience replay and live online testing in a reinforcement learning framework.

Dynamic pricing in oligopolies has multiple problems. One is the optimization problem, where we learn a Nash equilibrium policy when we are given the parameters of the market demand function, and the second one is learning the demand parameters themselves. For example, two studies used parametric approaches, with maximum likelihood to estimate the unknown parameters of the demand function. There is also recent research on demand learning, for example when there are multiple products and firms can learn to price on an assortment of items using multinomial logit regression, or when there are multiple products in a demand learning scenario and a limited inventory, where Multi-Armed Bandit approaches have been shown to be effective at finding profitable policies. But these approaches do not consider that past pricing actions influence the future market demand parameters. They also do not consider competing firms that aim for a Nash equilibrium.

- Our market setup
  - demand market where past pricing affects future market demand, in a market competition
  - multi-agent MDP; state transition driven by joint pricing actions of all players (firms)
  - simplifications: unlimited inventory per firm, single product, no substitutes

## 1.2 Multi-agent Markov Decision Processes

- Nash equilibria in Markov Games; oracle setting
  - Markov Games (MG's): important when agents self-interested, exact/approximate Nash desired
  - Nash computation hard: enormous joint state action space; approximations to the search exist
  - multiple Nash equilibria complicate the solution; some more desirable than others
  - approximate search: needs prior knowledge of joint reward function, often limited to two players, best response function
  - our payoff function as an oracle: parametric form known, agents don't know how rewards are generated
  - state visible to agents; state transition function unknown
  - demand parameters + Nash equilibria known for experimentation -> no pre-period model fitting; compare to theoretical solution, not empirical estimate

- Model-based vs model-free solvers
  - model-based approaches: provably find existence of a Nash equilibrium
  - we want model-free: no knowledge of reward or transition function
  - model-free algorithm for competitive MDP's when an external party can alter environment parameters - not always the case in market economics
  - model-free decentralized deep learning framework, agent blind to others' actions, proven Nash convergence
  - convergent solution for zero-sum MG's via entropy-regularization
  - both of the last two impose theoretical restrictions on the MG for convergence
  - provably convergent MG solver for imperfect information, restricted to two agents

- Contributions

## 1.1 Market Oligopoly

Ideally a firm's pricing strategy should take into account the actions of the other firms, and this is the justification for using Nash equilibrium policies instead of unilateral reward maximization policies. Others model market demand with parametric functions that have unknown parameters, but they do not consider a Nash equilibrium, and they also do not consider the effect of previous pricing actions on demand. So in almost all of the recent research on dynamic pricing under uncertainty there is a desideratum to compute and promote Nash equilibria for market pricing strategies. These kinds of strategies can be applied to eCommerce platforms like Amazon auto pricing, so that firms can opt for an automated pricing algorithm.

A large part of the dynamic pricing literature has assumed that the demand function is unknown and tried to learn the relationship between price and demand. It was shown that a myopic Bayesian policy can lead to incomplete learning and poor profit performance. A joint pricing and inventory problem has also been studied, where the price-sensitive demand is learned using a Bayesian dynamic program. Many recent studies are about non-parametric methods. For example, one pricing strategy balances the trade-off between exploration and exploitation. Also, in the deep reinforcement learning work mentioned above the demand function was a black box system and the demand was approximated from experience replay and live online testing in a reinforcement learning framework.

Dynamic pricing in oligopolies has multiple problems. One is the optimization problem, where we learn a Nash equilibrium policy when we are given the parameters of the market demand function, and the second one is learning the demand parameters themselves. For example, two studies used parametric approaches, with maximum likelihood to estimate the unknown parameters of the demand function. There is also recent research on demand learning, for example when there are multiple products and firms can learn to price on an assortment of items using multinomial logit regression, or when there are multiple products in a demand learning scenario and a limited inventory, where Multi-Armed Bandit approaches have been shown to be effective at finding profitable policies. But these approaches do not consider that past pricing actions influence the future market demand parameters. They also do not consider competing firms that aim for a Nash equilibrium.

We propose a demand market where the past pricing affects the future market demand in a market competition. To search for a Nash equilibrium we use a multi-agent Markov Decision Process, where the state transition is driven by the joint pricing actions of all the players (or firms). To make the problem simpler we assume that each firm has unlimited inventory and that there is only one product, with no substitutes.

## 1.2 Multi-agent Markov Decision Processes

Multi-agent Markov Decision Processes, or Markov Games (MG's), are an important research area, especially when there are multiple agents that are self-interested and an exact or approximate Nash equilibrium for the system is wanted. Computing Nash equilibria is also very difficult because the search is over the enormous joint state action space of the problem, although there are approximations to this search problem. Also, there can be multiple Nash equilibria, which makes the solution more complicated, since some solutions may be more desirable than others.

But approximate search algorithms need prior knowledge of the joint reward function and are often limited to two players, which are modelled by a best response function. We treat our payoff function as an oracle. This means that we know the parametric form of the payoff function, but the agents in the MG do not know how the reward function generates rewards for the players. The agents can see the state of the game, but they do not know the state transition function. However, for the purposes of experimentation the market demand parameters and the Nash equilibria are known. This removes the need for pre-period model fitting to pre-estimate market demand parameters, and lets us compare our solution to the theoretical solution instead of an empirical estimate.

There are also model-based approaches that can provably find the existence of a Nash equilibrium. But we want a Nash equilibrium solver that is model-free, where the agents do not know anything about the reward or the transition function. In recent literature, one model-free algorithm solves competitive MDP's when the environment parameters can be altered by an external party, but in market economics this is not always the case. Another work proposes a model-free decentralized deep learning framework where the agent is blind to the actions of the other agents, and convergence to a Nash equilibrium is proven. A convergent solution for zero-sum MG's via entropy-regularization has also been proposed. However, both of these works impose a number of theoretical restrictions on the MG in order for the convergence to happen. There is also a provably convergent MG solver for imperfect information, but it is restricted to two agents. We on the other hand are concerned with an approximate solution to a full information MG for N agents.

Contributions: In this work we outline a methodology for Deep Q Learning, which was introduced in earlier work, and we extend the framework to multi-agent reinforcement learning (MARL) with a Nash equilibrium objective, based on the methods of two other works. The framework in the first of these is theoretically sound, but the solution to the Nash equilibrium function is often intractable. So we use approximation methods to compute a Nash equilibrium. Black box optimization is applied to estimate an \epsilon -Nash Equilibrium policy, and this approximation is learned as a series of neural networks. We then apply this MARL model to the domain of dynamic pricing.

steps.text:
The application of deep reinforcement learning to single player Markov Decision Processes is relatively well-researched in today’s machine learning literature; however, applications of novel deep reinforcement learning methods to multi-agent competitive MDP’s are relatively few. In particular, the challenge revolves around competing objectives and solving for Nash equilibria [1], which are often computationally intractable, in a competitive setting where agents cannot simply maximize their own Q functions. Nash equilibria in Markov Games are particularly useful in the area of dynamic pricing, a well-known problem in today’s online eCommerce marketplaces. In a dynamic pricing game, multiple firms compete for market share of their product on the same online platform. To model this market, we adopt a modified version of Bertrand oligopoly [2], where the marginal cost of production is 0 and purchasing behaviour is probabilistic.

## 1.1 Market Oligopoly

Especially in today’s online commerce industries, dynamic pricing gives platform firms an adversarial advantage and increases profit margins in a competitive economy. Ideally, a firm’s pricing strategy should consider the actions of other firms, which justifies Nash equilibrium policies over unilateral reward maximization policies. In previous approaches, [3] modelled the dynamic pricing problem using deep reinforcement learning, but focused primarily on single agent revenue maximization rather than solving for multi-agent Nash equilibria. [4] apply stochastic dynamic programming in a simulated environment to estimate consumer demand and maximize expected profit, but do not consider the equilibrium solution of the market. [5] model market demand using parametric functions with unknown parameters, yet they consider neither a Nash equilibrium nor the effect of previous pricing on demand. Thus, in almost all recent research on dynamic pricing under uncertainty, there exists a desideratum to compute and promote Nash equilibria for market pricing strategies. Such strategies can be applied to eCommerce platforms such as Amazon auto pricing, allowing firms to opt for an automated pricing algorithm.

A large body of literature on dynamic pricing has assumed an unknown demand function and tried to learn the intrinsic relationship between price and demand. [6] showed that a myopic Bayesian policy may lead to incomplete learning and poor profit performance. [7] studied a joint pricing and inventory problem while learning the price-sensitive demand with a Bayesian dynamic program. Many recent studies have focused on non-parametric methods. [8] developed a pricing strategy that balances the trade-off between exploration and exploitation. Furthermore, in [3] the demand function was a black box system, and demand was approximated from experience replay and live online testing in a reinforcement learning framework.

Dynamic pricing in oligopolies presents multiple problems. One is the optimization problem, where we learn a Nash equilibrium policy given the parameters of the market demand function; the second is learning the demand parameters themselves. For example, [9] and [10] studied parametric approaches, using maximum likelihood to estimate the unknown parameters of the demand function. Recent research has also addressed demand learning, for example when multiple products exist and firms can learn to price on an assortment of items [11] using multinomial logit regression, or when multiple products and a limited inventory exist in a demand learning scenario, where Multi-Armed Bandit approaches have been shown to be effective at devising profitable policies [12]. However, these approaches do not consider past pricing actions influencing the future market demand parameters, nor do they consider competing firms aiming for a Nash equilibrium.

We propose a demand market where past pricing affects future market demand in a market competition. To search for a Nash equilibrium, we apply a multi-agent Markov Decision Process, where the state transition is driven by the joint pricing actions of all players (or firms). To simplify the problem, we assume that each firm has unlimited inventory and that there is only a single product with no substitutes.

## 1.2 Multi-agent Markov Decision Processes

Multi-agent Markov Decision Processes, or Markov Games (MG’s), are an important area of research, especially when multiple agents are self-interested and an exact or approximate Nash equilibrium for the system is desired. Computing Nash equilibria is additionally very difficult when searching over the enormous joint state action space of the problem, although approximations to this search problem exist [13]. Moreover, the existence of multiple Nash equilibria can further complicate the solution, since some solutions may be more desirable than others.

Yet approximate search algorithms require prior knowledge of the joint reward function and are often limited to two players, modelled by a best response function. We treat our payoff function as an oracle [14]: we know the parametric form of the payoff function, but the agents in the MG have no knowledge of how the reward function generates rewards for the players. The state of the game is visible to the agents, but they have no knowledge of the state transition function. Nevertheless, the market demand parameters and Nash equilibria are known for purposes of experimentation. This eliminates the need for pre-period model fitting to pre-estimate market demand parameters [15], allowing us to compare our solution to the theoretical solution rather than an empirical estimate.

Model-based approaches also exist that provably find the existence of a Nash equilibrium [16]. However, we aim for a model-free Nash equilibrium solver, where the agents have no knowledge of the reward or transition function. In recent literature, [17] present a model-free algorithm to solve competitive MDP’s when the environment parameters can be altered by an external party, but this is not always the case in market economics. Furthermore, [18] propose a model-free decentralized deep learning framework in which the agent is blind to the other agents’ actions, and prove convergence to a Nash equilibrium. [19] propose a convergent solution for zero-sum MG’s via entropy-regularization. However, both [19] and [18] impose a number of theoretical restrictions on the MG for this convergence to occur. Moreover, [20] present a provably convergent MG solver for imperfect information, restricted to two agents. We, in contrast, are concerned with an approximate solution to a full information MG for N agents.

Contributions: This work outlines a methodology for Deep Q Learning, as introduced in [21], extending the framework to multi-agent reinforcement learning (MARL) with a Nash equilibrium objective based on the methods in [22] and [23]. Although the framework in [22] is theoretically sound, the solution to the Nash equilibrium function is often intractable, so we apply approximation methods to compute a Nash equilibrium. Black box optimization is used to estimate an \epsilon -Nash Equilibrium policy, and this approximation is learned as a series of neural networks. The MARL model is then applied to the domain of dynamic pricing.
